## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Patrol officers and deputies who write incident reports from body-cam footage.
   [LYC] "Intros to Police, Sheriff, Transit, or University PDs that wrestle with video or paperwork overload."
   [LYC] "We auto-generate reports, verify narratives, and surface evidence instantly — cutting desk time by 60% and
   putting officers where communities need them most." → `roles[officer]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.
   Author's choice: "at small and mid-sized police departments" stands for [LYC]'s "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers)".

2. **What (the job).** Get every call written up as a report, accurately, without the officer stuck at the desk.
   [LYC] "40% of a typical shift vanishes to transcribing body-cam footage, filling forms, and locating clips across
   siloed systems." [YCW] "Officers spend up to a third of their shifts manually transcribing body camera footage".
   → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** After a call, when the footage has to become a report; at the desk, often past end of shift.
   [PR] (Chief Sever) "an officer might not be as detailed if they're 'down 10 reports'". [PR] "End-of-shift reports,
   which provide an overview of incidents over an entire shift, will continue to be written exclusively by humans."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: incident report`. Author's choice: the window {7, DAYS} (spec 120: "every shift"
   reads as 7 DAYS) and Frequency 3 to 5 days out of 7 (an officer works about four or five shifts in seven; the posts
   say "a typical shift", so every shift worked). Prevalence `p_80_100` follows from "a typical shift".

4. **Which people.** US police, sheriff, transit and university departments of 10 to 200 officers.
   [LYC] "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers) willing to co-shape features." [LYC] "We'll fly anywhere in North
   America to set you up within 48 hours—no strings attached." → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The department, per officer a month; the chief decides under a spending cap, the city council above it.
   [PR] "Sever said he's only able to authorize expenditures up to a certain amount without Heber City Council approval.
   Purchasing Draft One for around $30,000 per year would require such permission. Buying Code Four at around $6,000 to
   $8,000 per year would not." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: chief}`; Buyer and payer tests "Nobody else" (the
   chief alone), with "The city council" and "The city manager" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A side-by-side
   trial against Axon's tool", is from [PR] ("The Police Department recently completed free trial periods of two AI
   programs") and [CMP] ("We ran 30 days with Axon Draft One and 30 days with Code Four... 17/18 Officers chose Code Four
   at the end of the trial."); the other two items (a records-system check; the prosecutor's office agreeing) are the
   author's, the second from [BDN] (the district attorney: "It's not something that my office, or our PDs, have agreed
   is ready for use."). Commitment's step, "run a free pilot with a few officers": [LYC] "no strings attached"; [BDN]
   "he has provided a year of the software for free"; [PR] the free trial periods. Header: the outside payer (gap 2).

6. **Mechanism.** Footage in; a draft narrative in the department's format, each fact tied to its clip, with check
   words the officer must remove.
   [LYC] "Autofilled narrative reports that match your RMS schema and chain-of-custody rules." [LYC] "Real-time
   transcription & summarization — every body-cam or interview video becomes searchable text + key-frame timelined."
   [LYC] "One-click redaction — faces, plates, minors' voices, and PII are masked with CJIS-compliant logs."
   [BDN] (Cheng) "Essentially, we make it so that the patrol is reviewing the reports rather than writing the reports
   from scratch"; "Code Four inserts extraneous, random or incorrect information into the reports. If an officer doesn't
   remove that information, they cannot submit a final draft." [CMP] "Every report fact links to the source clip,
   transcript, and timestamp". → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (footage uploaded before
   the shift ends — tested; typed into the records system; time to read a draft) and Adoption friction (read and
   correct every draft — tested; delete the check words). Relative advantage's two benefits: [LYC] "cutting desk time
   by 60%" (shorter_time) and [CMP] "Code Four analyzes every frame of body camera footage, not just the audio"
   (less_worry); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $30 per officer a month; the cost is the officers' report time.
   [BI] "Cheng said Code Four works with 25 police departments and makes money via a subscription model, which starts
   at $30 per officer a month." [PR] "Code Four is significantly cheaper at $30 per officer per month. Sever estimated it
   would cost Heber City between $6,000 and $8,000 annually." → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $30 to $30 per officer
   (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, HOURS 40 to 60 of the incident reports per officer a month: author's arithmetic from [YCW] "up
   to a third of their shifts" and [LYC] "40% of a typical shift", on 8-to-10-hour shifts and about fifteen shifts a
   month (a third of 8 hours x 15 = 40; 40% of 10 hours x 15 = 60). The rate, $37 an hour, is [BLS] "The median annual
   wage for police and detectives was $77,310 in May 2025" ($37.17 an hour), the author's stand-in: no source gives an
   officer's hour. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [PR] (a Heber City sergeant, of a report drafted with an AI tool) "This report would have taken me an hour, and it
   took me eight minutes." [CMP] (a chief, vendor-curated) "Code Four helped one of my guys who was 3 weeks behind
   reports finish his reports" (the quote goes on; its last words are not reproduced here). [BDN] (a researcher) "There's
   a lot of error there because of background noise: being on the side of a highway, of trucks driving by".

## Status today

Widened, same core. [SITE] today sells four products (report writing, investigations over phone dumps and jail calls,
redaction, a mobile field-capture app) and claims "Live in 200+ departments"; [YCP] reads "Modernizing the police
workflow." Customer counts in the press: 25 departments ([BI] 2025-11-19), about 50 ([BDN] 2026-02-24). Price today:
no public price list ([SITE], read 2026-10-22); the latest dated figure is [BDN] "If the department decides to continue
using it, they will pay $50 per officer per month, or about $3,000 to $5,000 a year for the small department." (after a
free first year).

## Could not be sourced

- **A launch-era price.** Neither [LYC] nor the site's archived snapshot of 2025-07-01 carries one; the earliest dated
  price is [BI]'s $30 per officer a month, six months after launch. It is used as the founder's price because it is the
  nearest dated figure and the price the company named publicly first; a reader holding the entry to the launch era
  should treat the price as one step later than the rest.
- **An officer's hour.** No source gives one; [BLS]'s median for police and detectives stands in.
- **The hours per officer a month.** The founders give shares of a shift, not hours; the 40 to 60 is the author's
  arithmetic (item 7).
- **A buyer title for the cap.** Only Heber City's chief is on record ([PR]); that every chief has a cap, and that the
  council and city manager are the other roles, is the author's reading.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person officer accounts.** None exists; officer occasions are scripted from [PR], [BDN]
  and [CMP] (the last vendor-curated).
- The footage-upload condition (tested Compatibility), the three Purchase friction items but the trial, and every pick
  are the author's.

screens.why4: The three are distinct, cover how the draft fits an officer's work (footage in, report into the records system, time to review), and match the words I'd use, so choosing one is a real choice.
screens.why5: The picked condition appears word for word in the test, says what I believe about footage being up before end of shift, and the other two stay in the brief as promised.
screens.instead: Keep the question and options; reword the test as 'For most patrol officers, footage is uploaded before the shift ends' and the bar as 'Holds if at least 2 in 3 say a plain yes.'

screens.why1: Having said what it is and how it fits the way officers work, the obvious next thing is why an officer would switch from writing reports by hand.
screens.why2: The question is plain and I can answer it straight away in the words I use for my own pitch, and the 25-word limit is clear.
screens.why3: Desk time and what gets missed from the footage are exactly what I built this around and what I hear from departments.
screens.why4: The box takes my own benefits and the one chip, leaving this out of the study, is a fair escape because the test is optional.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my 'minutes, not an hour' but drops 'Nothing on the footage left out' and adds 'For most, their last call would have gone better', a claim I did not type.
screens.instead: Keep the question, and have the belief carry both benefits: 'For most, their last call's report would have been done in minutes, not an hour, with nothing on the footage left out.'

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better than today's way, Keel shows the benefits it drafted from that for me to check, so it is obvious why this screen is here.
screens.why2: The rows read like a cop would say them, but 'will tick from' takes a second read and 'their last call would have gone better' is off, because the call was over and only the report would have gone better.
screens.why3: I know what a report costs an officer and what our product changes, because that is the pitch I give chiefs every week.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in the trade's terms, but 'Nothing on the footage left out' is an absolute that no officer checking a draft could fully vouch for, and the pain I lead with, the backlog keeping officers at the desk past end of shift, has no row.
screens.why5: The benefits keep my meaning (faster reports, every frame analyzed), but my claim was 60% less desk time, 'minutes, not an hour' is sharper than that, and the belief tests only the first row although the intro says all are equal.
screens.instead: Title: What it does better than today's way. Rows: 'The report drafted in minutes, not an hour'; 'Details from the footage don't get missed'; 'Off the desk and home on time'. Keel will test: For most, their last report would have gone better with it.

screens.why1: After what it does better, I expect to be asked what it costs the officer in effort, so this question fits here as the fourth solution item.
screens.why2: It's plain on first read, and the hint's 'setup, extra steps or learning' tells me what kind of answer is wanted, though 'start using' fits the work on every report slightly less well than it fits setup.
screens.why3: I built the review step and the check words and have watched officers use them, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip beside a free-text box, and leaving this out is a fair choice for a founder who doesn't want to test friction.
screens.why5: The belief keeps 'read and correct every draft before signing' but this screen doesn't show the check words I also typed, which are the friction specific to Code Four.
screens.instead: What will officers have to do to use it, both to get started and on every report? Any setup, extra steps or learning. Up to 25 words.

screens.why1: Right after I said what officers must do to start, Keel shows the list back to check before choosing one to test, which is the obvious next step and the same pattern as the earlier solution checks.
screens.why2: Draft, signing, body-cam footage and check words are all plain to me as the founder of this product, and the instruction to reword, remove or add is clear on first reading.
screens.why3: I know exactly what an officer does with our tool, because I designed the review step and the inserted check words and I watch departments onboard.
screens.why4: The rows are distinct and in my words, but uploading footage is a per-call condition already tested under Compatibility rather than a new step to start using it, and nothing covers the actual start such as a short setup or training.
screens.why5: Reading and correcting every draft and deleting the check words is what I typed, and the belief that most would read and correct every draft keeps my meaning.
screens.instead: What they'll have to do: Read and correct every draft before signing; Find and delete the check words in each draft; Learn the tool in a short setup session.

screens.why1: After listing what officers must do to start using it, it makes sense to choose the one effort most likely to stop them, since strangers only get one question on it.
screens.why2: Drafts, signing and body-cam footage are everyday words in my trade, and 'check words' is my own term for what we insert, though 'nothing is reworded here' is a slightly odd aside.
screens.why3: I know this from pilots: officers' resistance comes from having to review every draft, remove the inserted errors and get footage uploaded, so I can pick without guessing.
screens.why4: All three are real efforts in my words and the true answer is there, but deleting the check words is really part of reading and correcting a draft, so those two overlap somewhat.
screens.why5: The list and the test keep what I typed: the officer reads and corrects every draft before signing, and the bar is clear.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? Read and correct every draft before signing, including deleting its check words / Upload the call's body-cam footage before the shift ends

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the obvious moment to decide whether to ask for a pilot, and free pilots are how I already get departments on board.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is the word I already use with departments, and the hint shows the exact line people will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Offering a no-strings trial is my own decision and I already make it, so I can answer at once.
screens.why4: Yes and no cover the whole choice, are distinct and read plainly, and an escape chip isn't needed for a founder's own yes-or-no decision.
screens.why5: The screen keeps my yes to a pilot, and "Would you try this for real?" fits the free trial I offer without misstating it, though the chief rather than an officer would approve a department's pilot.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, choosing who will put the questions to my officers is an obvious last step.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but 'Keel records the voice you pick once for this project: 400 credits' takes a second read because 'credits' is Keel's word, not mine, and the 'voice' here is really a face and voice on video.
screens.why3: I can listen to two five-second samples and decide which one I would put in front of patrol officers, with no guessing about anything outside what I know.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers, each with a sample and a default already picked, are complete and distinct for this choice, and no escape chip is needed because the choice has no 'don't know' answer.
screens.why5: It says 'patrol officers', my own word, and changes nothing of what I typed about the product or who it is for.
screens.instead: Who should ask patrol officers your questions? Daphne ▶ / Saskia ▶ -- with the hint saying 'Keel records this interviewer's face and voice once for this project; it costs 400 credits, whichever you choose.'

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions and just before sending, it makes obvious sense to settle how my officers will answer.
screens.why2: The choice itself is plain, but "Hear her," "Still recording," and "Ready when Daphne is" run together with the descriptions and take a second read to see they are a sample link and availability notes.
screens.why3: I know officers work on phones between calls, often in loud places such as a highway shoulder, so I can judge which format suits them.
screens.why4: The three options are complete and distinct, but "Let them choose" says "Daphne or text" where the option it refers to is called "Read and tap," and the transcription claim gives only a quiet-room and loud-room figure, which is an odd thing to weigh inside an option.
screens.why5: It keeps my "patrol officers" and shows "Read and tap," as I picked, without changing what my study means.
screens.instead: How should patrol officers answer? Options: Daphne, an AI interviewer (she asks aloud on video and each question is on screen; they talk, type or tap; ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap (they read each question and tap; they can speak or type in any box; ready now) / Let them choose (they pick Daphne or Read and tap when they open the link; ready when Daphne is).

screens.why1: Having just chosen how officers will answer and with the study ready to go out, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step.
screens.why2: The three choices read easily, but "People I found with Keel" and "the Contacts page" name a Keel feature and page I have not been shown in this flow, so that option takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know who I can reach: the officers at agencies I have met and the department groups where officers already gather, so I can answer this from my own outreach.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and my true answer of officers I know by name is there, but there is no way to mix routes or say I do not have the names yet, and a founder reaching officers through a chief would have to squeeze that into the first option.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes what I typed; my pick of people I know by name is kept, and the flow's wording does not alter my study.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? People I know by name (I send each one their own link) / People I find with Keel's contact search (pick a list; Keel makes a link for each, and I send them) / A group with one open link (I post it where they already are; each person signs in with Google, then is interviewed).

screens.why_b1: The verdict, 'Too few to call', is stated at the top, and each card ties it to its deciding number: 4 answered, 5 needed.
screens.why_b2: This page has no chart, and while the cards plainly show 4 counted against a bar of 5, it takes a second look to square that with '7 people answered' because nothing says why 3 dropped out.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction each carry the exact belief line I checked on the way in, in my words about footage uploaded before shift end, minutes not an hour, and reading every draft.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need more answers, but the page never says so or what this means for the idea, such as how many more officers to ask or which ones.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the answers: the low n is said outright, 4 of 7 stays visible, and no belief is called held or failed.
screens.instead: None of your three beliefs can be called yet: 7 officers answered but only 4 could be counted on each because [reason], so get at least one more countable answer per belief before you trust or change anything about the solution.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside the number that decides it, 4 counted with 5 needed, and the So line repeats it, though the header's "4 answered" is loose against the count line's "5 answered, 4 counted".
screens.why_b2: The counts (3 yes, 1 with some steps, 0 no) and the four people counted are plain, but "3 of 4" next to "against your bar" took me a second look because it reads like my result when all 4 count for me and it is really the bar.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and the line about footage uploaded before the shift ended are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" tells me not to lean on this, but it does not tell me to get at least one more usable answer or say what the early lean means for requiring footage uploaded before the shift ends.
screens.why_b5: The small group is called out as "a lean, not a call", n stays visible, Luis's guess is left out with the reason given, and nothing is claimed about officers beyond these people.
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 officers counted had their footage uploaded before the shift ended, 0 had not, but I need at least 5 counted (the bar: no more than 1 in 3 say no), so get one more clear answer before relying on footage being there by end of shift.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" and the deciding number are both there, but the verdict's "4 answered" disagrees with the count line's "5 answered · 4 counted", so with 5 needed and 5 names listed I have to read down to see that the shortfall is one uncounted guess.
screens.why_b2: Better 3 and Same 1 of 4 read at once, but the bar takes a second look because it is given as both "3 of 4" and "no more than 1 in 3", on a strip with a fifth ghost cell.
screens.why_b3: The name Relative advantage and the line about the report done in minutes, not an hour, are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is honest but generic: it shows I am one counted answer short without telling me to get one more officer's account of a specific call or what this means for the idea.
screens.why_b5: It makes no claim beyond the people who answered: it refuses a call even though 3 of 4 reaches the bar, says the group is small, and flags the answer as a hypothetical.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 5 officers answered but Luis's answer was a guess, so 4 count and 5 are needed; 3 of the 4 said a lot better, a lean only, so get one more officer to walk through a real last call before relying on it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict "Too few to call" sits beside the number that decides it, and the So line ties them together as 4 counted, 5 needed, though the header's "4 answered" loosely conflicts with the count line's "5 answered · 4 counted".
screens.why_b2: The four answers, all for, and the bar at 3 of 4 are plain, but I need a second look to see that the ghost cell is the missing fifth person or Luis, and why clearing a 3-of-4 bar still doesn't make a call.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and "Most would read and correct every draft before signing" are what I checked on the way in, and the question uses my product's name.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" implies I need one more counted officer but doesn't say so, and it doesn't tell me what to do about the two officers who would only do it on a condition.
screens.why_b5: It makes no claim beyond these officers: the small group is called "a lean, not a call", Luis's guess is left out with the reason given, and the two conditional yeses are shown as conditional.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of the 5 who answered were counted, and you need 5. All 4 would read and correct every draft, 2 of them only on a condition, so get one more officer's clear answer and ask what would make it worth it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits directly above its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no answer yet and exactly why, though the screen's why is only one officer's.
screens.why_b3: 'Relative advantage' and 'the report done in minutes, not an hour' are the dimension name and belief line I checked on the way in, unchanged.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for the idea or what to do next, not even to get one more answer so the line can be called, and the stray 'No difference / against' at the bottom leaves me to work it out.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the people who answered: the 4 of 5 shortfall is stated, the group is counted at 1, and the single quote is shown as one person's words.
screens.why_b6: Kenji's quote adds two things I did not type, that simple reports already get done in the car between calls and that staffing is what makes people wait, but it is one voice and its theme label 'On their own' says little.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 answered, 1 more needed. The one officer against says simple reports already get written in the car and being two cars short is the real problem, so get one more answer and ask whether the saving shows up on long reports like DUI arrests rather than simple ones.

screens.why1: It's the first screen and I can see why a study would check my department's size before asking about my work, though the 'A recent time' label doesn't match a size question.
screens.why2: Officers and department are the words I use every day, and I can answer on one read.
screens.why3: I know roughly how many sworn officers my department has, so I can answer without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it with nothing odd or missing, and a screener like this needs no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the 10 to 200 officer size and shows nothing of a product or the founder's terms; it doesn't name police, sheriff, transit or university departments, but 'officers' covers mine.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two plain options and the numbers say well, so I could answer after hearing it once.

screens.why1: Right after checking my department's size, it makes sense to ask whether I recently wrote a report late, because that sets up the story about my last call.
screens.why2: I get it on first read, but I'd say "shift" rather than "tour" and "incident report" rather than "call report".
screens.why3: I know whether I stayed past clock-out to finish a report this week, because it happens often enough that I remember.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a yes-or-no gate shouldn't carry two escape chips, and "I can't recall one particular call" doesn't fit because the question is about the whole week, not one call.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product leaks, but the founder's situation of turning body-cam footage into a report has narrowed to finishing after the shift, so an officer who writes up footage on shift gets screened out.
screens.why6: It's one short question ending in "Yes or no," and I could answer it after hearing it once.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you finish an incident report after your shift ended? Yes / No (no escape chips)

screens.why1: I just said I finished a report after my tour ended, so being shown an idea about drafting reports from body-cam footage makes obvious sense here.
screens.why2: Body-cam, narrative, records format, redact and sign are all my daily words, but "adds check words you must catch" I had to read twice, and I only guess it means planted errors or markers to prove I actually read it.
screens.why3: I upload body-cam, write narratives and sign reports every shift, so I can picture this against my own calls.
screens.why4: It is a card to read with no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: It is a plainly labelled idea card that keeps one clear meaning, and the name and product are shown on purpose with no internal language about me or my role.
screens.why6: It says fine in short sentences and I would follow most of it once, but "a drafted report from footage" is a clumsy opener, "check words you must catch" will not land on one hearing, and the redaction and search line tacks on extras to hold.
screens.instead: Imagine Code Four, a tool that drafts your report from body-cam footage. You upload a call's footage and it writes the narrative from the video and audio, in your department's records format. It links every fact to its clip and plants test words you have to catch, so you know you read it, then you review and sign. It can also redact footage in one click and search across it. The people building it believe you would review and sign instead of writing from scratch.

screens.why1: Right after hearing about a report drafted from footage, it makes sense to ask whether my footage was already uploaded by the end of my shift.
screens.why2: Last call, uploaded footage and end of shift are all how I talk about the job, so I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: I know whether my camera got docked, but it often uploads by itself at the dock around end of tour, so on my last call I may be guessing whether it finished before I went off shift.
screens.why4: Yes and No fit and I can't tell works if the dock did the upload, but "Yes, with some steps" is odd for something that either had happened or hadn't, and it doesn't clearly mean docking the camera or tagging the clips by hand.
screens.why5: The idea card is shown on purpose, and the question stays on my footage and my shift with no product plans or company terms for people like me reaching me.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is short, one question with three options I can hold and one escape at the end, so I could answer after one hearing.
screens.instead: Think of your last call. Was its footage uploaded before your shift ended? Yes, it uploaded by itself; Yes, I docked or uploaded it myself; No, it uploaded after my shift. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the card and the upload question, it makes sense to ask whether this thing would have helped on the call I just thought about.
screens.why2: The words are easy, but 'go better' is a little loose because the call itself would go the same and only the report afterward could change, so I have to work out that that's what it means.
screens.why3: I know my last call and how long the report took, but all I've been told is 'a drafted report from footage', so I'd be partly guessing how good the draft would be.
screens.why4: Lot better, little better, no difference and worse cover it in words I'd use, and 'I can't tell' is the honest out if I haven't seen the draft.
screens.why5: It's the idea card shown on purpose and the question asks only whether it would have helped, with no pitch or company talk reaching me.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four short options I can hold after one hearing and a single escape at the end.
screens.instead: Would Code Four have made writing the report from your last call better for you, or not? A lot better; a little better; no difference; or worse. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: After being shown the idea and asked if it would have helped, it makes sense to ask whether I'd do the one thing it demands of me, checking the draft before I sign.
screens.why2: Draft, correct and sign are how I already talk about a report going to my sergeant, so I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: I sign my name to every report and I know how I'd treat a draft I'm legally answerable for.
screens.why4: The four cover it and the escape fits, but 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' is odd here because I have to review anything I sign anyway, and it blurs into plain 'Yes' without saying worth what.
screens.why5: It keeps to the idea on the card and the review step it requires, with no plans, pitch or company terms for people reaching me.
screens.why6: Heard once it is short, one question, with four short options I can hold and the escape said last.
screens.instead: To use Code Four, you'd read and correct every draft before you sign it. Would you do that, or not? Yes; Yes, if it saved me time overall; Probably not; No; or I can't tell.
